strengths: The core idea is attractive: replacing iterative NeRF retraining for viewpoint uncertainty estimation with a lightweight feedforward network (UPNet) that maps a single image to a full uncertainty map over candidate viewpoints, enabling a ~400x speedup and large reductions in CPU/RAM/GPU usage — a practically meaningful result for AVS pipelines.

A substantial new resource: the NUM dataset (62,400 viewpoint–UMap pairs across 13 ShapeNet categories, 4 uncertainty metrics), which the authors commit to releasing along with code and models, supporting reproducibility and follow-up research.

Fairly broad empirical validation: in-domain and out-of-domain (held-out category) settings, three random seeds with standard deviations reported, two different downstream rendering models (NeRF and 3DGS), and thorough ablations covering uncertainty metrics, redundancy/aggregation policies, and the instance-diversity vs. viewpoint-density trade-off.

The finding that viewpoints selected via a PSNR-trained UPNet transfer across rendering models and even to unseen categories is a genuinely useful empirical result, and the ablations provide reasonable design justification for the selection policy.
The paper is well written and well organized, with clear task formalization (polar UMap over spherical viewpoints) and a transparent experimental protocol shared across all methods.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to synthetic, center-aligned ShapeNet objects on a fixed-radius sphere with known geometry. Despite motivating AVS via robotics, search-and-rescue, etc., there are no real-world or cluttered-scene experiments, which limits the significance of the claims. The paper acknowledges this only in the Discussion.

The claimed 'comparable to the all-views upper bound with half the views' is overstated: e.g., in the ID setting PUN's PSNR is 33.19 vs. 36.47 for the upper bound (a ~3.3 dB gap), and OOD results are similarly below the upper bound on most metrics. 'Comparable' is not supported by the numbers shown.

Novelty is more incremental than presented. Supervised/RL next-best-view learning already exists ([31], [48]); the contribution is largely the shift from predicting a discrete next view to predicting a continuous uncertainty map. Moreover, UPNet still predicts over a fixed 48-anchor set with angular-distance interpolation, so the claimed generalization to 'arbitrary viewpoints' rests on a coarse 48-point discretization plus a hand-crafted interpolation heuristic.

Ground-truth UMaps are defined as the reconstruction errors of one specific single-view synthesis model (Splatter-Image), so UPNet arguably learns the failure modes/biases of that particular backbone rather than intrinsic scene uncertainty. The transfer experiments mitigate but do not eliminate this concern, and no baseline tests a simpler uncertainty proxy (e.g., predicting Splatter-Image error directly with a regression baseline, or ensemble-based uncertainty).

The compute-efficiency comparison (Table 2) is inherently favorable: baselines retrain a rendering model after every selection while PUN does not; the speedup is a property of the paradigm rather than a like-for-like algorithmic comparison. Also, recent 3DGS-based AVS methods discussed in related work (ActiveSplat, ActiveGS, ActiveGAMER) are cited but not compared empirically.

Several methodological details are under-specified or inconsistent: the redundancy-removal threshold of 0.1 is applied to UMap values that are said to be PSNR-based and unnormalized (where a 0.1 threshold would be nearly vacuous); the multiplicative aggregation of PSNR-like values over timesteps lacks justification; and the soft-decision policy appears somewhat heuristic.

The very large margins over baselines with 3DGS (36.71 vs. 30.67 PSNR in Table 3) raise questions about whether baselines were optimally adapted to the 3DGS setting, given their uncertainty heuristics were designed for NeRF.

OOD evaluation covers only 2 held-out categories with 10 instances each, and UPNet depends on ImageNet-pretrained ViT features whose category-level priors may contribute to generalization in ways that are not disentangled.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and well-motivated problem (active view selection for 3D reconstruction) and identifies a genuine inefficiency in existing pipelines that retrain a neural rendering model at each step.

The core idea is clean and interpretable: predicting a neural uncertainty map over candidate viewpoints from a single image with a lightweight feedforward network (UPNet), then aggregating maps over time to suppress redundant views.

The evaluation is fairly thorough: in-domain and out-of-domain (novel category) settings, three metric families (image quality, mesh quality, visual coverage), multiple baselines (WD, A-NeRF, NVF), two downstream rendering models (NeRF, 3DGS), and multiple ablations (uncertainty metric, selection policy, dataset composition).
The compute-efficiency results are convincing: ~400x speedup and large reductions in CPU/RAM/GPU usage for viewpoint selection are well documented with repeated runs and standard deviations.
The NUM dataset (62,400 viewpoint–UMap pairs across 13 ShapeNet categories) and promised code/model release are useful contributions to the community.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: learning a direct mapping from current view to next-best-view via supervised learning already exists (e.g., [31, 48]), and PUN largely swaps the target of prediction (UMap over anchors instead of a discrete next-view label). The technical contribution amounts to fine-tuning an ImageNet-pretrained ViT with an MSE loss to regress a 48-dimensional vector, plus a hand-crafted aggregation heuristic (thresholding + multiplicative accumulation).

The 'uncertainty' is not principled: ground-truth UMaps are just reconstruction errors (PSNR, etc.) of one specific single-view synthesis backbone (Splatter-Image) at 48 anchors. This ties the supervision to the idiosyncrasies of a particular model and metric rather than to genuine epistemic/aleatoric uncertainty, and it is unclear why this transfers to unrelated rendering models, beyond the empirical results.

Evaluation is confined to synthetic, center-aligned ShapeNet objects on a spherical manifold with fixed radius. Real-world applicability—objects off-center, arbitrary radii, cluttered scenes, real captures—is untested and acknowledged only in the discussion. The claim of generalization to 'novel object categories' is based on only 2 unseen categories with 10 instances each, which is a thin basis for a strong generalization claim.

Improvements over the strongest baseline (NVF) are marginal in the ID setting (e.g., PSNR 33.19 ± 1.74 vs. 33.08 ± 0.44; SSIM tied), and the reported standard deviations are large relative to the gaps, weakening the claim that PUN 'consistently outperforms all baselines' on all seven metrics.

The 400x speedup comparison is somewhat expected rather than surprising: baselines retrain a NeRF at every step while PUN runs a single ViT forward pass; a more informative comparison would include efficient learned-NBV baselines [31, 48] re-implemented in the same setting, which are missing.

Several design choices appear ad hoc and weakly justified: the 0.1 redundancy threshold, the 30-degree interpolation neighborhood, softmax-weighted angular-distance interpolation, and multiplicative aggregation—each is ablated only superficially, and no theoretical or information-theoretic grounding for the selection rule is provided.

The 'comparable to the all-views upper bound using half the views' framing is flattering: the upper bound trains and evaluates on the same 40 poses, an idealized setting; the more meaningful gap (e.g., PSNR 33.2 vs. 36.5) is downplayed.

Fairness concerns: PUN benefits from category-level priors learned from ShapeNet training data, while baselines (WD, A-NeRF, NVF) are category-agnostic; this asymmetry should be discussed more explicitly when interpreting the OOD results.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practical problem (active view selection for 3D reconstruction) and identifies a real limitation of existing NeRF/3DGS-based AVS pipelines: the need to retrain a rendering model after each view is added.

The core idea is clean and effective: a lightweight feedforward network (UPNet) that maps a single input image to a neural uncertainty map over candidate viewpoints, removing the need for iterative rendering-model training at selection time. This yields a very large and convincingly measured efficiency win (Tab. 2: ~400x speedup, large reductions in CPU/RAM/GPU usage).

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: two neural rendering backbones (NeRF and 3DGS), in-domain and out-of-domain category splits, three metric families (image quality, mesh quality, visual coverage), multiple competitive baselines (WD, A-NeRF, NVF), three seeds with standard deviations, and a reasonable upper-bound reference.

The ablation studies (Tab. 4 / Tab. S2) are informative and cover the key design axes: uncertainty metric choice, redundancy-removal and aggregation policies, and the instance-diversity vs. viewpoint-density trade-off in training data.

The contribution of a new large-scale Neural Uncertainty Map (NUM) dataset (13 ShapeNet categories, 62,400 viewpoint–UMap pairs) is a useful community resource, and the authors commit to releasing code, models, and data.
The paper demonstrates that viewpoints selected by PUN transfer across rendering models and to unseen categories without retraining, supporting the claim of generalization.

The paper is clearly written, with a well-illustrated problem setup (Fig. 1, Fig. 2) and honest discussion of limitations (single-object spherical viewpoint assumption, image-reconstruction-based uncertainty).
weaknesses: The gains over the strongest baseline (NVF) in the in-domain setting are small (e.g., 33.19 vs. 33.08 PSNR, 6.96 vs. 6.98 MSE), and in some cases NVF matches or slightly beats PUN (e.g., CR). The headline 'outperforms all baselines across all seven metrics' claim is technically true but the margins are within noise for several ID metrics; the more convincing gains are in OOD and 3DGS settings.

The evaluation is entirely on synthetic, center-aligned ShapeNet objects with a spherical camera distribution at fixed radius. Real-world applicability, cluttered scenes, or non-normalized objects is untested, and this significantly narrows the claimed significance of AVS for 'real-world applications' cited in the introduction.

There is a potential evaluation bias: the ground-truth UMaps used to train UPNet are derived from PSNR error, and PSNR is also the primary evaluation metric, which may favor PUN's selection strategy on that metric. The ablation showing metric choice has limited effect (Tab. 4a) partially mitigates this, but a discussion is warranted.

Several components of the method are hand-crafted and somewhat ad hoc (0.1 uncertainty threshold for redundancy removal, 30-degree neighborhood for softmax interpolation, multiplicative aggregation across timesteps). While ablated, the sensitivity of results to these hyperparameters is not fully characterized.

The 400x speedup comparison is somewhat expected by construction: PUN replaces iterative NeRF retraining with a single feedforward pass, so the comparison with methods designed for a different regime, while practically useful, does not isolate a like-for-like algorithmic improvement.
The OOD evaluation uses only 2 unseen categories with 10 test instances each, which is a small sample for strong generalization claims.

Novelty is moderate: learning a direct mapping to next-best-view has been explored via supervised learning [31] and RL [48]; the main novelty is the uncertainty-map output representation and its aggregation, which is an incremental but well-executed contribution.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('UnkowN', 'epoche', 'diable' in Tab. S2), the main-text ablation table (Tab. 4) reports only PSNR despite seven metrics being discussed, and some baseline setups (fixed 512 candidates for baselines vs. random 512 per step for PUN) differ subtly.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated and clearly written; the idea of predicting a reconstruction-error-based uncertainty map with a lightweight feedforward network to avoid costly per-step NeRF/3DGS retraining is a practical and useful contribution to the AVS literature.

Comprehensive evaluation: multiple datasets (NUM variants, NeRFAssets, MIP360), multiple reconstruction backbones (NeRF, 3DGS, Binocular3DGS), several strong baselines (WD, A-NeRF, NVF, Uniform), and an extensive set of ablations (uncertainty metric, selection policy, dataset composition, anchor count, redundancy threshold).
Large measured efficiency gains are convincingly documented (Table S4): 0.5 min vs 175+ min for viewpoint selection with drastically lower CPU/RAM/GPU usage, which is practically significant.

Generalization is addressed more carefully than in many prior works: held-out categories, altered lighting, changed camera distance, and real scenes, plus analysis (Sec. 5.2/E, Tables S7, Fig. S5) explaining why the learned uncertainty transfers across backbones.
Release of the NUM dataset (62,400 viewpoint-UMap pairs) and code/models supports reproducibility; multi-run reporting with standard deviations.
weaknesses: The headline claim that PUN 'achieves comparable reconstruction accuracy' to the all-views upper bound is overstated: on NUM-inst the gap is ~3.3 dB PSNR (33.19 vs 36.47), and the upper bound itself is an idealized setup where training and evaluation views coincide. 'Comparable' should be softened or justified.

Novelty is moderate: the core method reduces to supervised fine-tuning of a ViT on ground-truth error maps plus heuristic interpolation and product aggregation over timesteps. Learned next-best-view prediction exists (Mendoza et al. 2020, RL-NBV), and the main contribution is the specific uncertainty-map formulation rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Improvements over the strongest baseline NVF are small on NUM-inst (e.g., PSNR 33.19 vs 33.08 with std 1.74, SSIM ties) and statistical significance is not assessed; only NUM-cat and the 3DGS-recon setting show clearly larger gains.

Comparison to recent 3DGS-based active reconstruction methods discussed in the related work (ActiveSplat, ActiveGS, ActiveGAMER) is missing; all evaluated baselines are NeRF-centric, and on NeRFAssets/MIP360 only NVF is compared.

Results on real scenes are thin: only 4 instances each from NeRFAssets and MIP360, with relatively low absolute quality (e.g., PSNR 17.49 on MIP360), making it hard to judge robustness in truly unconstrained settings; the method also assumes object-centered spherical viewpoints, limiting scope (acknowledged in the discussion).

Ground-truth UMaps are defined by reconstruction error of a single synthesis model (Splatter-Image); while backbone-robustness ablations help, there is residual circularity and PSNR-based uncertainty may under-weight geometric fidelity (also acknowledged).
Some presentation inconsistencies (e.g., MSE scaling conventions across Table 1/S1, minor typos such as 'diable', empty URL in the reproducibility statement) reduce polish.

strengths: The core idea is clean and practically motivated: replacing costly per-step NeRF/3DGS retraining with a lightweight feedforward network (UPNet) that predicts a full uncertainty map over candidate viewpoints from a single image. This yields genuine and well-documented compute savings (Tab. S4: ~400x faster selection, large reductions in CPU/RAM/GPU).

The paper contributes a large-scale Neural Uncertainty Map (NUM) dataset (13 categories x 100 instances x 48 viewpoints with UMaps from four uncertainty metrics), which is a reusable resource for the AVS community.

Evaluation is broad: held-out instances, held-out categories, varied lighting (NUM-light), varied camera distance (NUM-cam-dist), alternative reconstruction backbones (3DGS, Binocular3DGS), and real scenes (NeRFAssets, MIP360), with multiple runs and standard deviations reported.

Thorough ablations covering uncertainty metrics, selection/aggregation policies, dataset composition (instance diversity vs. viewpoint density), anchor count, and redundancy threshold, plus an analysis (Sec. 5.2, Tab. S7) explaining why single-view reconstruction error is a reasonable proxy for viewpoint difficulty.
The paper is generally well written and organized, with an honest discussion section that acknowledges limitations (image-based uncertainty, spherical viewpoint assumption).
weaknesses: Improvements over the strongest baseline (NVF) are often marginal and within noise. On NUM-inst, Ours achieves PSNR 33.19 (1.74) vs. NVF 33.08 (0.44) and identical SSIM; on NUM-light, mesh/visibility metrics are actually worse (Acc 0.31 vs 0.34, Vis 0.43 vs 0.44). The claimed advantage is not convincingly established on the primary benchmark.

The headline claim of 'reconstruction accuracy comparable to the all-views upper bound using half the views' is overstated: the gap is ~3.3 dB PSNR (33.19 vs 36.47 on NUM-inst; 34.74 vs 36.91 on NUM-cat), which is a substantial difference in novel view synthesis, not 'comparable.'

Missing comparisons with recent state-of-the-art 3DGS-based AVS methods that the paper itself discusses in detail (ActiveSplat, ActiveGS, ActiveGAMER). The evaluated baselines are all NeRF-entropy/variance-style methods from 2022-2024, weakening the SOTA claim.

The method inherits strong assumptions: viewpoints restricted to a sphere at fixed radius r=2.73m around a single, centered, normalized object; UMaps anchored to one single-view synthesis backbone (Splatter-Image) trained on ShapeNet. Real-scene results (MIP360: PSNR 17.49, SSIM 0.29) are weak in absolute terms and only compared against a single baseline (NVF).

The core proxy assumption - that single-view reconstruction error predicts multi-view reconstruction informativeness - is supported only by moderate correlations (|r| up to ~0.6, Tab. S7) with generic view-complexity cues. The claimed 'domain-agnostic' and backbone-agnostic behavior is argued narratively rather than demonstrated rigorously, and the theory-level justification for multiplying uncertainties across timesteps is ad hoc.
On NeRFAssets, PUN beats NVF on image metrics but loses on completion ratio (0.47 vs 0.51) and visibility (0.424 vs 0.457), partially contradicting the claimed superiority on geometry-aware metrics.

Novelty is incremental: supervised learning of next-best-view mappings exists (Mendoza et al. 2020; RL-NBV 2024); the contribution is reformulating the target as a viewpoint-wise uncertainty map, which is a sensible but not conceptually groundbreaking step.

Presentation issues: inconsistencies and typos in the ablation tables (e.g., 'diable+last'), the reproducibility statement and abstract end with an empty URL placeholder, and several quantitative claims (e.g., '400x speedup', 'over 50% reductions') are highlighted in the abstract without noting they apply only against retraining-based baselines, which is expected by construction.
Statistical significance of the reported gains is not analyzed; given overlapping standard deviations across many metrics, several 'best' entries may not be meaningfully better.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practical problem (active view selection for 3D reconstruction) and identifies a genuine weakness in prior art: the heavy computational cost of retraining NeRF/3DGS models at each selection step.

The core idea is clean and novel in its combination: learning a direct feedforward mapping (UPNet) from a single view to a full uncertainty map over candidate viewpoints, followed by simple interpolation, filtering, and multiplicative aggregation across timesteps. This avoids per-step model retraining and yields large efficiency gains (reported 400x speedup, large reductions in CPU/RAM/GPU), which is a meaningful practical contribution.
The authors contribute a new large-scale resource: the NUM dataset (62,400 viewpoint–UMap pairs across 13 ShapeNet categories with 4 uncertainty metrics), which could be useful to the community.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: multiple datasets (synthetic ShapeNet variants, NeRFAssets, MIP360), multiple reconstruction backbones (NeRF, 3DGS, Binocular3DGS), multiple metric families (image quality, mesh quality, visual coverage), and extensive ablations (uncertainty metric, selection policy, aggregation, dataset size, anchor count, redundancy threshold).

Generalization is tested seriously: novel object categories, changed lighting, changed camera distance, and real-world scenes, all without retraining; a correlation analysis (Pearson r=0.82) plus a view-complexity analysis provides some insight into why the method transfers.
Reproducibility appears strong: training details, splits, seeds, hardware, and a statement that all code/models/datasets will be released.
weaknesses: The central claim that PUN achieves 'comparable reconstruction accuracy' to the upper bound with half the views is overstated. Table 1 shows a persistent gap of roughly 3+ dB PSNR (33.19 vs 36.47 on NUM-inst; 34.74 vs 36.91 on NUM-cat) and worse LPIPS/MSE. The method is clearly better than baselines, but 'comparable to upper bound' is stronger than the evidence supports and should be toned down.

Comparison to the most relevant recent 3DGS-based active methods (ActiveSplat, ActiveGS, ActiveGAMER) is missing despite these being cited in the related work; baselines are limited to NeRF-uncertainty methods (WD, A-NeRF, NVF) and Uniform. Given the paper's positioning around compute efficiency and 3DGS, this comparison gap is notable.

The approach is tightly constrained to object-centric, spherical viewpoint distributions at a fixed radius (r=2.73m) around a single object; MIP360/NeRFAssets results require adaptation (e.g., re-centering views) and performance there is weaker relative to the synthetic setting. The discussion acknowledges this, but it limits the claimed generality for unconstrained AVS.

Statistical support for headline improvements is uneven: on NUM-inst the gain over NVF in PSNR is small (33.19 vs 33.08) relative to reported std (~0.44–1.74), and on NUM-cat the large standard deviations (up to ~2.8) make some conclusions less robust; significance testing is not reported.

The supervision signal derives uncertainty from single-view synthesis errors of one specific backbone (Splatter-Image) on ShapeNet-style objects; the argument that this transfers across backbones is supported empirically (Tabs. S2/S3) but is somewhat heuristic, and the claim of backbone-agnosticism rests on limited subsets (e.g., 50 airplane instances for PUN-NeRF).

Some design choices are heuristically motivated rather than principled (multiplicative aggregation across timesteps, 0.1 redundancy threshold, 30-degree interpolation kernel), and while ablations cover them, the ablation differences are often small relative to variance.

Writing contains minor issues, e.g., the reproducibility statement gives an empty URL, some table formatting in Table 3 is hard to parse, and terminology (uncertainty vs. reconstruction error) is conflated at times—the 'uncertainty' is really a predicted reconstruction error, not a calibrated uncertainty estimate.
